content.title: About
content.content: Pork is the meat of domestic pigs, and a pork steak (NS) refers to a cut that is grilled or pan‑seared. It has a mild flavor, moderate fat content, and the characteristic aroma of pork. The steak is usually served as a main dish and can be paired with a variety of sauces and sides.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
NS pork steak is often cut from the loin or shoulder, giving it a tender texture.
Different cultures feature pork in traditional dishes ranging from barbecue to roasts.
Pork provides all essential amino acids needed by humans.
When cooked properly, the steak retains most of its nutrients.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork steak supplies high‑quality protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B1, B3, B6 and B12, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is essential for immune function, wound healing, and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: The iron in pork is highly bioavailable and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: In moderate amounts, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats in pork support heart health.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or Trichinella.

items.title: Allergy and sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may react to pork proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed versions
items.content: Marinated or smoked steaks can be high in salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the pork steak to medium doneness, slice against the grain, and serve with vegetables, potatoes or whole‑grain sides. Complement with yogurt‑based, mustard or tomato sauces for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh steak refrigerated at 0–4 °C for no more than 2–3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for 4–6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Red salsa is a spicy sauce made from ripe tomatoes, red peppers, onion, garlic, vinegar and spices. It has a bright, slightly hot flavor with hints of sweetness and acidity, perfect for Mexican dishes, snacks and grilled foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally salsa is prepared with fresh ingredients without cooking.
The red color comes from ripe red tomatoes and/or red chili peppers.
Salsa is often used as a low‑calorie alternative to richer sauces and dressings.
In Mexico salsa is served with almost every meal, from tacos to grilled fish.
There are many regional salsa variations that differ in heat level and spice blend.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes, the main ingredient, contain lycopene – a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and skin.

items.title: Vitamins C and A
items.content: Salsa provides vitamin C for immunity and vitamin A for vision.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: One tablespoon of salsa contains about 10–15 kcal, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Capsaicin from red peppers stimulates gastric secretions and may aid digestion.

items.title: Probiotic content
items.content: Fermented salsa can contain beneficial bacteria that promote gut health.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: High heat may irritate the stomach of people with sensitive digestive systems.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to tomatoes or peppers, which can cause skin or gastrointestinal reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salsa often contains added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Store‑bought salsa may contain preservatives and sweeteners that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use salsa as a dip for chips, veggie sticks, shrimp, and as a topping for tacos, burritos, grilled meat, fish or chicken. It can be added to marinades, salads, or used as a base for soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep salsa in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator. Once opened, it lasts 1–2 weeks. Discard if it develops off‑odors or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Tea, iced, brewed, black, unsweetened is a refreshing beverage made from black tea leaves brewed with hot water and then chilled. It contains no added sugar, preserving the natural bitterness and aroma of black tea while being low in calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is the most consumed tea worldwide after green tea.
Cooling brewed tea retains most antioxidants such as polyphenols.
Iced tea is often served with a slice of lemon or lime to enhance flavor.
Unlike many ready‑to‑drink beverages, iced brewed tea contains no preservatives or artificial flavors.
The term “iced tea” originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became a summer staple.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Black tea provides polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular consumption of black tea may help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: Caffeine in black tea boosts alertness and cognitive performance.

items.title: Sugar‑free hydration
items.content: Unsweetened iced tea supplies fluid without extra calories.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Tannins in black tea can help regulate digestion and reduce bloating.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience nervousness, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Iron absorption
items.content: Tannins can reduce the absorption of non‑heme iron from plant foods, so it’s best to drink tea between meals.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Frequent consumption may increase stomach acidity in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the iced brewed black tea chilled over ice. Optionally add a slice of lemon, lime, or fresh mint. If desired, sweeten lightly with honey or stevia, but the classic version contains no added sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared iced tea in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it becomes cloudy, develops an off‑taste, or smells stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Whey protein is a high‑quality protein derived from milk whey after the curd is separated. The dry, sweet version usually contains added flavorings and sweeteners, making it convenient for protein shakes and baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whey protein is considered a complete protein: it contains all essential amino acids.
Dry whey has a longer shelf life compared with liquid forms.
Sweet varieties are often fortified with B‑vitamins and minerals to support metabolism.
Whey is a by‑product of cheese production, improving overall food industry efficiency.
It dissolves quickly in water, making it easy to consume right after a workout.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: Rich in amino acids, especially leucine, it stimulates muscle‑protein synthesis after exercise.

items.title: Accelerates recovery
items.content: Protein replenishes amino‑acid stores lost during training, reducing muscle soreness.

items.title: Aids weight management
items.content: High protein content increases satiety and helps preserve lean mass during calorie restriction.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Whey contains immunoglobulins and lactoferrin, which may enhance the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Improves body composition
items.content: Regular intake combined with training helps lower body‑fat percentage while increasing muscle mass.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy may experience adverse reactions.

items.title: Excessive protein intake
items.content: Too much protein can strain kidneys and liver, especially in individuals with pre‑existing conditions.

items.title: Sweetener content
items.content: Sweetened versions often contain artificial sweeteners that may cause discomfort for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Added additives
items.content: Some brands include flavorings and colorants that might be undesirable for clean‑eating diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix 30 g of whey with 200–250 ml of water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage. It can also be added to smoothies, oatmeal, cottage cheese, or used in baking to boost protein content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the bag tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption.
